title: doj asks us supreme court allow trump ally remain nevadas top federal prosecutor 2026 09 09
text:
Sept 9 (Reuters) - The Trump administration is asking the U.S. Supreme Court to condone its efforts to bypass the usual processes to appoint new leaders for U.S. Attorney's Offices nationwide, after a federal appeals court ruled that Sigal Chattah is not validly serving as the lead federal prosecutor in Nevada.
The ​administration in a petition filed on Tuesday asked the justices to overturn a decision last month by the San Francisco-based 9th ‌U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals that disqualified Chattah from supervising three criminal cases after finding that she was unlawfully appointed.
Two other federal appeals courts have handed down similar rulings in recent months, concluding that Trump allies were unlawfully installed to lead U.S. Attorney's Offices without U.S. Senate approval.
Solicitor General D. John Sauer in the petition said the three ​rulings conflict with the Federal Vacancies Reform Act, which he said the executive branch has long interpreted to allow the attorney general ​to delegate power when various offices are vacant.
He argued the lower courts' rulings "risk chaos" and would leave future presidential administrations "with ⁠few good options for acting officers to safeguard critical posts pending confirmation of permanent replacements."
"More immediately, the decision below threatens to inject mass confusion ​into five U.S. Attorney’s Offices in the Ninth Circuit that collectively handle over 8,000 civil and criminal cases annually," Sauer argued. "This Court’s swift intervention is ​warranted to put that uncertainty to rest."
The case arises from the administration's efforts to install top prosecutors without going through the Senate, where the so-called "blue slip" policy gives Democratic senators an effective veto over picks in their home states they do not favor.
Chattah, who served as Nevada's chairwoman for the Republican National Committee prior to joining the ​U.S. Department of Justice, was appointed in late March 2025 to serve a 120-day stint as interim U.S. Attorney in Nevada.
When her tenure was ​about to expire around July 26, then-Attorney General Pam Bondi extended her appointment under a different federal law and made her acting U.S. Attorney, effectively preempting judges in her ‌district from ⁠appointing an interim U.S. Attorney pending Senate confirmation of a new top prosecutor.
Bondi designated Chattah as the First Assistant U.S. Attorney for the District of Nevada, the No. 2 for the office. Under the Federal Vacancies Reform Act of 1998, the person in that position would serve as acting U.S. Attorney.
Federal public defenders in Nevada brought the legal challenge to Chattah's authority in several separate criminal cases. They argued she should be disqualified because her appointment ​was unlawful and asked for the ​cases to be dismissed.
U.S. District ⁠Judge David Campbell agreed in September, prompting the Trump administration to appeal to the 9th Circuit, which ruled that a first assistant U.S. Attorney can only serve as head of the office under the federal vacancies law if ​that person held the position at the time the vacancy arose.
The Philadelphia-based 3rd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ​and the New ⁠York-based 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals have issued similar rulings holding that Trump allies Alina Habba and John Sarcone were unlawfully appointed as the top federal prosecutors in New Jersey and the Northern District of New York, respectively.
The case is United States v. Jackson, U.S. Supreme Court, No. 26-304.
For the United States: Solicitor General ⁠D. John ​Sauer
